topics: Linear inequalities in one or two variables

body.en: A linear function models a constant rate of change; an inequality describes a region rather than a single line.

For \( f(x)=mx+b \), \( m \) is the rate and \( b \) the starting value. Parallel lines share a slope; perpendicular slopes multiply to \( -1 \). An inequality's boundary line is dashed for \( < \) or \( > \), solid for \( \le \) or \( \ge \).
Adjust the slope \( m \) and intercept \( b \) of \( y=mx+b \). The amber dots mark the intercepts the SAT most often asks for.

label.en: ⚠️ SAT Traps & Pitfalls — Rate of Change & Inequality Half-Planes

body.en:
• Rate of Change Multiplier Trap: When a question states 'the depth increases by $3$ cm for every $10$ minutes', the slope is $\frac{3}{10} = 0.3$, NOT $3$. Pay close attention to the denominator units!
  • Initial Value Confusion: The $y$-intercept ($x = 0$) represents the starting value before any change occurs. If a word problem measures time $t$ in years since 2010, the year 2015 corresponds to $t = 5$, NOT $t = 2015$.
  • Dashed vs. Solid Boundary Lines: Strict inequalities ($<$ or $>$) require dashed lines (boundary points excluded); inclusive inequalities ($\le$ or $\ge$) use solid lines (boundary included).
  • Test-Point Method for Inequalities: Always test $(0, 0)$ in the inequality. If $(0,0)$ satisfies the statement, shade the region containing $(0,0)$; if false, shade the opposite half-plane.

label.en: Exam Practice 2.C — Interpreting Linear Slope & Intercept

body.en:
Question: An ecologist models the population $P$ of trout in a lake as $P(t) = 1400 - 35t$, where $t$ is the number of years after 2015. What is the best interpretation of the number $35$ in this model?

Solution: The model is in linear form $P(t) = mt + b$, where $b = 1400$ is the initial population in year 2015, and $m = -35$ is the rate of change. The negative sign indicates a decrease. Therefore, $35$ represents the estimated decrease in the trout population for each one-year increase in time.

label.en: Exam Practice 2.D — System of Linear Inequalities

body.en:
Question: Which ordered pair $(x, y)$ is a solution to the system of inequalities $y > 2x - 3$ and $y \le -x + 4$?

Solution: Test the candidate point $(1, 2)$:

  1. First inequality: $2 > 2(1) - 3 \implies 2 > -1$ (True).
  2. Second inequality: $2 \le -(1) + 4 \implies 2 \le 3$ (True).

Since $(1, 2)$ satisfies both inequalities simultaneously, it lies within the feasible solution region.
